scenarioNames.target-c: Target C · weak alpha, more delta

awake.title: Awake · fast mixed activity
awake.morph: Irregular, rather low-amplitude activity with fast beta components; frontal EMG can overlap.
awake.when: Before induction, during light sedation or during emergence.
awake.meaning: Awake activity is variable and is not defined by a single frequency peak.
awake.influence: Eye state, attention, age, EMG and electrode contact.
awake.drugNote: The awake reference is used for comparison. A similarly fast pattern under ketamine, midazolam or EMG does not prove wakefulness.

alpha.title: Alpha · 8–13 Hz
alpha.morph: Rhythmic activity with about 8 to 13 oscillations per second.
alpha.when: Often frontal under propofol and together with slow/delta.
alpha.meaning: Typical part of the propofol alpha/delta complex.
alpha.influence: Propofol effect, age, baseline EEG and derivation.
alpha.drugNote: Propofol can markedly strengthen frontal alpha together with slow/delta. At very deep effect, continuous alpha structure decreases again.

delta.title: Delta · 0.5–4 Hz
delta.morph: Very slow waves, usually with high amplitude.
delta.when: Sleep, sedation and deep hypnotic effect.
delta.influence: Sedation, cerebral function, age and metabolism.
delta.drugNote: Propofol, sevoflurane and dexmedetomidine can strengthen slow/delta. Stronger opioid effect can also slow the EEG, but does not replace hypnosis assessment.

theta.title: Theta · 4–8 Hz
theta.morph: Medium-slow activity with about 4 to 8 oscillations per second.
theta.when: Transitions, sleep proximity and several sedatives.
theta.meaning: Less specific than a clear alpha/delta complex.
theta.influence: Sedative, sleep-wake state and baseline activity.
theta.drugNote: Theta can increase under sevoflurane, midazolam and dexmedetomidine. The band is unspecific and must be assessed with the other frequencies.

beta.title: Beta · 13–30 Hz
beta.morph: Fast activity, usually with lower amplitude.
beta.when: Awake state, arousal, benzodiazepines or ketamine.
beta.meaning: Fast activity does not automatically mean wakefulness.
beta.influence: EMG, midazolam, ketamine, arousal and electrode contact.
beta.drugNote: Midazolam can emphasize beta. Low-dose ketamine often produces fast activity around 25–32 Hz.

gamma.title: Gamma · 30–45 Hz
gamma.when: Activation, EMG influence and typical ketamine patterns.
gamma.meaning: Gamma in the frontal signal is especially artifact-prone.
gamma.influence: Ketamine, muscle activity, movement and electrode contact.
gamma.drugNote: Ketamine can create high-beta/low-gamma activity. EMG and artifacts must be excluded before interpretation.

spindle.title: Spindles · 12–16 Hz
spindle.morph: Rhythmic sigma packets lasting about 1–2 seconds, waxing and waning.
spindle.when: Typical in sleep-like sedation under dexmedetomidine.
spindle.meaning: Visible in the DSA as intermittent narrow power islands.
spindle.influence: Dexmedetomidine dose, vigilance, baseline EEG and derivation.
spindle.drugNote: Dexmedetomidine can produce spindle-like 12–16 Hz episodes with slow/delta; at deeper effect the slow activity usually becomes stronger.

arousal.title: Arousal · beta activation
arousal.morph: Brief weakening of stable slow/alpha activity with an increase in fast 12–25 Hz activity.
arousal.when: Activation, emergence or reaction to an internal or external stimulus.
arousal.meaning: An arousal is a change over time, but not reliable proof of wakefulness.
arousal.influence: Sedation depth, stimuli, analgesia, EMG, movement and baseline EEG.
arousal.drugNote: Under propofol, arousal can appear as alpha dropout, fast beta activation or another pattern. Always include clinical context and artifacts.

alphaDropout.title: Alpha dropout · transient stimulus response
alphaDropout.morph: Temporary weakening or interruption of frontal 8–13 Hz alpha activity while baseline activity persists.
alphaDropout.when: Can occur after a nociceptive or other activating stimulus.
alphaDropout.meaning: Loss of an alpha peak is a trend change, not direct proof of pain or wakefulness.
alphaDropout.influence: Stimulus, analgesia, hypnotic depth, age, derivation and artifacts.
alphaDropout.drugNote: Under GABAergic anesthetics, a stable frontal alpha peak can temporarily decrease during a stimulus response.

deltaArousal.title: Paradoxical delta arousal
deltaArousal.morph: Transient increase in slow delta activity, often together with a decrease in alpha or spindle activity.
deltaArousal.when: Mainly described as a possible stimulus response during deeper general anesthesia.
deltaArousal.meaning: In this context, more slow activity can indicate a reaction and not simply deepening.
deltaArousal.influence: Stimulus strength, hypnotic depth, analgesia, drug and baseline EEG.
deltaArousal.drugNote: Delta arousal can leave processed hypnosis indices unchanged or lower them. Read raw EEG, DSA and clinical course together.

emg.title: EMG / muscle artifact
emg.morph: Irregular broadband fast activity, often rougher and less rhythmic than cortical beta activity.
emg.when: Forehead tension, movement, shaking, jaw activity or insufficient electrode stability.
emg.meaning: Can artificially increase high-frequency DSA power and processed indices.
emg.influence: Muscle activity, movement, electrode position and filtering.
emg.drugNote: Before adjusting a dose after a sudden index increase, check EMG, signal quality, raw EEG and clinical signs.

mixed.title: Alpha/delta complex
mixed.morph: Slow delta wave with superimposed rhythmic alpha activity.
mixed.when: Typical frontal propofol pattern during continuous hypnosis.
mixed.meaning: Two separate power maxima: slow/delta and alpha.
mixed.influence: Propofol effect, age, dose trend and derivation.
mixed.drugNote: The alpha/delta complex is a typical propofol signature. Combinations with opioids can change the required hypnotic effect and the trend.

suppression.title: Suppression
suppression.morph: Very low activity, partly alternating with bursts.
suppression.when: Very deep cerebral depression or targeted therapy.
suppression.influence: Sedatives, cerebral condition, temperature and metabolism.
suppression.drugNote: High hypnotic effect, for example from propofol or volatile anesthetics, can trigger discontinuity up to burst suppression.

game.discovery.sequenceProgress: Progress through the illustrative EEG sequence
game.discovery.watch: Watch the raw EEG and the one-minute DSA together.
game.discovery.aboutPatient: This fictional patient has early severe ARDS. The team has documented a temporary RASS −4 goal for controlled ventilation while preparing prone positioning. This is an individual scenario, not a sedation target for every patient with ARDS. No neuromuscular blockade is present during the RASS assessments.
game.discovery.aboutSuppression: Deep sedation and burst suppression are different observations. RASS −4 or −5 does not define an EEG pattern. Suppression is not intended in this case; specific neurological indications require their own specialist plan.
game.discovery.aboutSequence: The 60-second sequence is a teaching illustration, not the time course of a drug or a patient recording. The shared simulator generates the signals. Indices are hidden because the story does not establish a numerical RASS–qCON conversion. Alpha/delta activity is an example in this propofol context, not a universal target.
game.discovery.aboutReview: The reassessment illustrates what the team would review together. No dose or treatment interval is calculated. A frontal EEG display complements clinical assessment; it does not provide a complete neurological diagnosis or establish analgesia.
game.discovery.title.3: Reassess the patient and the goal.
game.discovery.heading.0: What can the clinical assessment tell us?
game.discovery.copy.0: Our focus is the brain. EEG helps us observe propofol's effect on brain activity, alongside the clinical response. Explore the bedside context, then add the EEG.
game.discovery.heading.1: Deep sedation does not mean burst suppression.
game.discovery.copy.1: This reference shows continuous alpha/delta activity. The clinical RASS is −4 in our story. EEG and the clinical score describe different aspects of the patient's state.
game.discovery.heading.2: Watch the quiet intervals become longer.
game.discovery.copy.2: The sequence develops gradually over 60 seconds. This change may occur without a different RASS score. Check signal quality, treatment timing and other causes; do not deepen sedation just to obtain a lower number.
game.discovery.heading.3: Same clinical score. A more continuous pattern.
game.discovery.copy.3: After reviewing signal quality, possible causes and the treatment plan, the team reassesses. This illustrative endpoint combines RASS −4 with continuous EEG. The display does not calculate how to get there.
game.discovery.label: DISCOVER EEG
game.discovery.noConversion: Illustrative EEG · No fixed RASS–qCON conversion
game.discovery.fictional: A fictional ICU case · No quiz, no timer
game.room.text.0: Early severe ARDS. For this patient, the team has chosen temporary deep sedation to support controlled, lung-protective ventilation. Prone positioning is being prepared.
game.room.text.1: For clarity, this example shows propofol alone, delivered intravenously. It does not depict a complete ICU treatment. EEG helps us observe the effect on brain activity alongside the clinical assessment.
game.room.text.2: No response to voice; movement to physical stimulation. There is no neuromuscular blockade in this teaching case. This assessment does not tell us whether the EEG is continuous or suppressed.
game.room.illustration: Illustrative ICU scene. Propofol is delivered by a separate Agilia-style syringe pump through an IV line to the patient's hand. The breathing circuit connects the mouth to the ventilator. A bedside monitor shows ECG and oxygenation traces.
game.room.caption: Intubated · IV propofol · Proning planned
game.guide.topic.0.label: Why EEG?
game.guide.topic.0.title: Observe the brain during sedation.
game.guide.topic.0.text: Propofol changes brain activity. EEG helps us observe that effect continuously, alongside the patient's clinical response. Blood pressure and ventilator behaviour remain important, but do not directly show the EEG pattern.
game.guide.topic.0.note: The simulator's alpha/delta example shows continuous activity. Deep sedation does not require burst suppression.

game.guide.topic.1.label: Why in ICU?
game.guide.topic.1.title: Follow a changing clinical situation.
game.guide.topic.1.text: The reason for sedation can change during an ICU stay. EEG and DSA can reveal changes in continuity between clinical assessments, including unexpected suppression. Interpret the pattern with signal quality, medications and the patient's condition.
game.guide.topic.1.note: Clinical assessment and EEG-derived indices describe different information. There is no fixed RASS-to-qCON conversion.

game.guide.topic.2.title: From the sensor to the screen.
game.guide.topic.2.text: A disposable forehead sensor with three electrodes records the EEG. A patient cable connects it to the monitor, which brings the waveform, spectrogram and processed indices together.
game.guide.topic.2.note: Conox supports monitoring during anaesthesia and sedation. It is not a diagnostic EEG system, and its indices alone do not determine a drug dose.

game.paths.discover.title: Discover EEG
game.paths.discover.description: See what EEG adds to a clinical assessment. One step at a time.
game.paths.discover.outcome: Get comfortable with the display and its main functions.
game.missions.discover-signal.title: Meet Conox
game.missions.discover-signal.intro: Start with the quality of the signal.
game.missions.discover-signal.prompt: Find SQI and EEG / DSA. Select both to locate them on the monitor.
game.missions.discover-signal.scene: Your first look at the Conox display. Explore an existing simulator reference signal.
game.missions.discover-signal.guide: Start with the measurement: SQI describes signal quality; EEG shows the signal itself.
game.missions.discover-signal.question: What should accompany your first look at the indices?
game.missions.discover-signal.takeaway: Conox brings indices and signal information together. Start by checking the measurement before interpreting the numbers.
game.missions.discover-signal.reference: IFU §3.8–3.11 · Signal quality, EEG and impedance.
game.missions.discover-signal.options.a.label: Read qCON only.
game.missions.discover-signal.options.a.feedb: The surrounding information helps you assess the measurement.
game.missions.discover-signal.options.b.label: Check the signal quality, electrode contact and the EEG.
game.missions.discover-signal.options.c.label: Treat SQI as a sedation score.
game.missions.discover-signal.options.c.feedb: SQI describes signal quality, not sedation.
game.missions.discover-indices.title: Two numbers, two questions
game.missions.discover-indices.intro: Give qCON and qNOX their own roles.
game.missions.discover-indices.prompt: Match each index to the information it is designed to provide.
game.missions.discover-indices.scene: The two large indices answer different questions. Their values are not interchangeable.
game.missions.discover-indices.guide: qCON relates to consciousness. qNOX relates to the probability of response to a noxious stimulus.
game.missions.discover-indices.question: How would you use these two indices together?
game.missions.discover-indices.takeaway: qCON and qNOX provide two complementary pieces of information on one display.
game.missions.discover-indices.options.a.labe: Use either number; they mean the same thing.
game.missions.discover-indices.options.a.feed: The two indices have different intended functions.
game.missions.discover-indices.options.b.labe: Read each for its own purpose, alongside the signal and clinical assessment.
game.missions.discover-indices.options.c.labe: Read qNOX as a pain-intensity score.
game.missions.discover-indices.options.c.feed: qNOX is not a measure of perceived pain intensity.
game.missions.discover-display.title: Look beyond the number
game.missions.discover-display.prompt: Find the BSR and the EEG / DSA. Select both to see where they appear.
game.missions.discover-display.scene: This existing simulator example contains bursts and quieter intervals. It is a pattern exercise, not a patient treatment target.
game.missions.discover-display.guide: BSR summarises suppression. The raw EEG lets you examine the alternating activity.
game.missions.discover-display.question: What does BSR describe?
game.missions.discover-display.takeaway: The EEG and BSR help you recognise suppression rather than relying on a single consciousness value.
game.missions.discover-display.options.a.feed: BSR describes EEG suppression, not analgesia.
game.missions.discover-display.options.b.labe: The proportion of flat EEG in the monitor’s analysis window.
game.missions.discover-display.options.c.labe: A score that should always be maximised.
game.missions.discover-display.options.c.feed: Suppression is a finding to interpret in context, not a universal goal.
game.missions.discover-advisory.title: Try the qCON advisory
game.missions.discover-advisory.intro: Turn it on and see a threshold crossing.
game.missions.discover-advisory.prompt: Enable the advisory. Lower the upper limit below the displayed qCON to trigger a visual reminder.
game.missions.discover-advisory.scene: A controls demonstration using the simulator’s existing limits. These settings are not clinical targets. No sound is required for this exercise.
game.missions.discover-advisory.guide: The advisory is linked to qCON. Change the upper limit while watching the qCON area.
game.missions.discover-advisory.question: What does the advisory tell you?
game.missions.discover-advisory.takeaway: Configurable qCON limits provide an additional visual and acoustic reminder. They support, rather than replace, active monitoring.
game.missions.discover-advisory.options.a.lab: It provides a diagnosis and a drug dose.
game.missions.discover-advisory.options.a.fee: A threshold crossing is not a prescription or diagnosis.
game.missions.discover-advisory.options.b.lab: qCON has crossed a configured limit; assess the signal and patient.
game.missions.discover-advisory.options.c.lab: It allows the patient to be monitored unattended.
game.missions.discover-advisory.options.c.fee: The IFU excludes using this advisory for unattended parameter monitoring.
game.paths.explore.title: Explore Conox
game.paths.explore.description: Put the Conox features to work. Connect the numbers, patterns and context.
game.paths.explore.outcome: Practise reading the information together in an ICU learning context.
game.missions.explore-goal.title: Agree the sedation goal
game.missions.explore-goal.intro: Give the team a shared language.
game.missions.explore-goal.prompt: Select qCON and EEG / DSA to review alongside the documented clinical target.
game.missions.explore-goal.scene: At handover, a colleague proposes converting the displayed qCON directly into a RASS score. The team needs to agree what this patient requires and how it will reassess that goal.
game.missions.explore-goal.guide: RASS assesses the response to stimulation. qCON is an EEG-derived index. Read them together without treating them as the same scale.
game.missions.explore-goal.question: How would you describe the goal at handover?
game.missions.explore-goal.takeaway: A shared goal includes its clinical reason and when it will be reviewed. qCON adds a trend to that conversation; it does not assign a RASS score.
game.missions.explore-goal.reference: qCON–RASS observational study · No universal conversion.
game.missions.explore-goal.options.a.label: Use qCON 65 as a universal equivalent of RASS −2.
game.missions.explore-goal.options.a.feedback: The relationship varies across patients, drugs and conditions. There is no fixed conversion.
game.missions.explore-goal.options.b.label: State the clinical target and its reason, then discuss the index, EEG and patient response together.
game.missions.explore-goal.options.c.label: Aim for the lowest possible qCON in every ventilated patient.
game.missions.explore-goal.options.c.feedback: The target follows the current treatment situation; a lower number is not automatically better.
game.missions.explore-trends.title: Put changes on a timeline
game.missions.explore-trends.intro: Connect the display with treatment events.
game.missions.explore-trends.prompt: Open “All signals” to see EEG, DSA and index trends together.
game.missions.explore-trends.scene: At handover, the team asks when the EEG changed in relation to care, boluses or infusion adjustments. Practise finding the combined view on this reference display.
game.missions.explore-trends.guide: The raw EEG shows the current pattern. DSA and index trends help locate changes over time; clinical event times must be checked separately.
game.missions.explore-trends.question: What makes a trend useful for reviewing sedation?
game.missions.explore-trends.takeaway: Use the timeline to ask when a change began and what else happened. Review drug delivery, medication effects and the patient before explaining a changing dose–effect relationship.
game.missions.explore-trends.reference: ICU pEEG consensus · Raw EEG, spectrogram and clinical context.
game.missions.explore-trends.options.a.label: Use the lowest index alone to calculate the correct infusion rate.
game.missions.explore-trends.options.a.feedba: The display does not calculate an individual dose.
game.missions.explore-trends.options.b.label: Compare EEG and index changes with the timing of treatment and assessments.
game.missions.explore-trends.options.c.label: Diagnose drug tolerance or a ceiling effect from a plateau alone.
game.missions.explore-trends.options.c.feedba: A mismatch between dose and observed effect prompts a broader review; a plateau does not establish its cause.
game.missions.explore-awakening.title: Prepare an awakening trial
game.missions.explore-awakening.intro: Revisit the goal as the situation changes.
game.missions.explore-awakening.prompt: Select qCON and EEG / DSA as additional observations during a planned reassessment.
game.missions.explore-awakening.scene: Later in the ICU stay, the acute reason for deep sedation has resolved. The team is considering an awakening trial and first checks its local safety criteria.
game.missions.explore-awakening.guide: Observe responsiveness and tolerance alongside the EEG and trend. A higher index does not establish orientation or readiness for extubation.
game.missions.explore-awakening.question: How can EEG monitoring contribute to this trial?
game.missions.explore-awakening.takeaway: Reassess the reason for sedation as the clinical situation evolves. EEG is an additional observation during a supervised trial, not its eligibility or stopping rule.
game.missions.explore-awakening.reference: AHRQ · Coordinated awakening and breathing trials.
game.missions.explore-awakening.options.a.lab: Start an awakening trial as soon as qCON reaches a fixed number.
game.missions.explore-awakening.options.a.fee: Eligibility is a clinical decision; a numerical threshold does not replace the safety screen.
game.missions.explore-awakening.options.b.lab: Add the EEG and index trend to clinical reassessment after the safety screen, using the team’s trial protocol.
game.missions.explore-awakening.options.c.lab: Treat the EEG as a guarantee that the patient can be extubated.
game.missions.explore-awakening.options.c.fee: Awakening and breathing readiness require their own assessments.
game.missions.explore-suppression.title: Deep does not mean suppressed
game.missions.explore-suppression.intro: Compare continuity, early gaps and suppression.
game.missions.explore-suppression.prompt: Explore all three references. Compare continuity in the EEG with BSR and DSA.
game.missions.explore-suppression.scene: Deep sedation may coexist with continuous activity. These three independent examples make the distinction from emerging discontinuity and longer suppressed intervals visible.
game.missions.explore-suppression.guide: Watch each pattern over several seconds. Quieter intervals lengthen across the examples; the comparison is not a drug-dose response.
game.missions.explore-suppression.question: Does a RASS of −4 or −5 require burst suppression?
game.missions.explore-suppression.takeaway: Check whether suppression is intended. If it is unexpected, review the signal, possible causes and treatment goal with the team. Specific neurological indications need a separate specialist plan.
game.missions.explore-suppression.reference: ICU pEEG consensus · Recognising and interpreting suppression.
game.missions.explore-suppression.options.a.l: Yes, burst suppression confirms the target for every deeply sedated patient.
game.missions.explore-suppression.options.a.f: Deep sedation is not a universal indication for suppression.
game.missions.explore-suppression.options.b.l: No. The clinical response and the EEG pattern are separate observations; suppression needs its own context.
game.missions.explore-suppression.options.c.l: No, because a continuous EEG proves the patient is awake.
game.missions.explore-suppression.options.c.f: Continuous alpha/delta activity can occur with deep sedation in this context.
game.paths.challenge.title: Conox Challenges
game.paths.challenge.description: Read the whole picture. Investigate clues and explain your decisions.
game.paths.challenge.outcome: Test your observation and reasoning with familiar simulator patterns.
game.missions.challenge-artefact.title: Look beyond ventilator tolerance
game.missions.challenge-artefact.intro: Investigate a cough, movement and fast activity.
game.missions.challenge-artefact.prompt: Choose the pair of clues that helps separate muscle activity from the EEG.
game.missions.challenge-artefact.scene: Another patient on pressure support triggers breaths, coughs and intermittently becomes asynchronous. Fast activity appears on the display. These signs need investigation, not an automatic increase in sedation.
game.missions.challenge-artefact.guide: Movement and EMG may contribute to fast activity and higher indices. Neither synchrony nor a high number alone establishes the patient’s conscious experience.
game.missions.challenge-artefact.question: What should happen before interpreting the index rise?
game.missions.challenge-artefact.takeaway: Ventilator behaviour and haemodynamics are clinical clues. EEG adds information about brain activity; none of these observations should be turned into a diagnosis on its own.
game.missions.challenge-artefact.reference: ICU pEEG consensus · EMG, artefacts and interpretation.
game.missions.challenge-artefact.options.a.la: Assume coughing proves pain and deepen sedation immediately.
game.missions.challenge-artefact.options.a.fe: Cough and asynchrony have several possible causes, including tube irritation; assess them in context.
game.missions.challenge-artefact.options.b.la: Assess the patient, breathing interaction and signal quality; compare EMG with the raw EEG.
game.missions.challenge-artefact.options.c.la: Treat stable heart rate and SpO₂ as proof that sedation is adequate.
game.missions.challenge-artefact.options.c.fe: These values matter for patient safety, but are not direct measures of sedation depth.
game.missions.challenge-context.title: Read the whole picture
game.missions.challenge-context.intro: Bring medication context into the interpretation.
game.missions.challenge-context.prompt: Select two display elements to review alongside the medication context.
game.missions.challenge-context.scene: This is the existing propofol/ketamine example from the simulator. Review the index and signal together.
game.missions.challenge-context.guide: The IFU describes a possible rise in the indices with ketamine that is not linked to the anaesthetic state.
game.missions.challenge-context.question: How should a higher index be interpreted in this context?
game.missions.challenge-context.takeaway: Medication context matters. A number must be interpreted alongside the information that can influence it.
game.missions.challenge-context.options.a.lab: The index proves a return of consciousness.
game.missions.challenge-context.options.a.fee: The medication context prevents that conclusion from the index alone.
game.missions.challenge-context.options.b.lab: Consider the medication effect, the signal and the patient before concluding wakefulness.
game.missions.challenge-context.options.c.lab: Ignore all EEG information once ketamine is involved.
game.missions.challenge-context.options.c.fee: The signal still contributes to a broader assessment.
game.missions.challenge-change.title: Notice the early gaps
game.missions.challenge-change.intro: Recognise a change before assuming its cause.
game.missions.challenge-change.prompt: Inspect all three references. Find the intermediate pattern as well as the marked suppression.
game.missions.challenge-change.scene: A clinical RASS assessment can remain unchanged while EEG continuity changes. These reference patterns let you practise noticing that difference.
game.missions.challenge-change.guide: Look for the early interruptions, then the longer quieter periods. A gradual change and an abrupt change after a bolus need a review of their timing and possible causes.
game.missions.challenge-change.question: What does a new discontinuous pattern justify?
game.missions.challenge-change.takeaway: Describe what changed before explaining why. EEG and DSA make changes in continuity visible; the patient and treatment history determine their meaning.
game.missions.challenge-change.reference: ICU pEEG consensus · Continuous observation and signal context.
game.missions.challenge-change.options.a.labe: Conclude that the clinical assessment is useless.
game.missions.challenge-change.options.a.feed: The assessment describes the clinical response; EEG adds complementary information between assessments.
game.missions.challenge-change.options.b.labe: Check signal quality, the treatment timeline and other causes, then reassess the agreed sedation goal.
game.missions.challenge-change.options.c.labe: Conclude that a specific propofol bolus must be the cause.
game.missions.challenge-change.options.c.feed: Timing can suggest an association, but the pattern alone does not establish a drug or dose as its cause.
game.missions.challenge-reason.title: Make a useful handover
game.missions.challenge-reason.intro: Explain the goal, the evidence and the next check.
game.missions.challenge-reason.prompt: Beyond the indices, choose the pair that adds signal quality and the underlying EEG pattern.
game.missions.challenge-reason.scene: A colleague reports stable blood pressure, heart rate and SpO₂. The team also needs to know the sedation goal, clinical response and what the brain monitoring has shown.
game.missions.challenge-reason.guide: Haemodynamics reflect illness and drugs as well as other influences. They do not replace assessment of sedation or the EEG.
game.missions.challenge-reason.question: Which handover gives the team a useful shared picture?
game.missions.challenge-reason.takeaway: Monitor the function you want to understand. Brain monitoring complements clinical assessment; a frontal EEG display is not a complete neurological diagnosis. Keep the clinical goal explicit.
game.missions.challenge-reason.options.a.labe: Stable blood pressure means the sedation target is met.
game.missions.challenge-reason.options.a.feed: Blood pressure is useful context, not a sedation-depth measurement.
game.missions.challenge-reason.options.b.labe: Explain why sedation is needed, the clinical target and response, signal quality, EEG/index trends and the reassessment plan.
game.missions.challenge-reason.options.c.labe: The qCON advisory has not activated, so there is nothing to reassess.
game.missions.challenge-reason.options.c.feed: A configured reminder complements active observation; it cannot confirm a complete clinical assessment.
